title: 169 Years Later, a Famous Court Case About Freedom Still Echoes Today
summary:
What if you went to court to ask for your freedom, and the highest court in the land said no — because of the color of your skin? That’s exactly what happened to Dred Scott in 1857. He was an enslaved man who sued for his freedom, but the Supreme Court ruled against him. The decision was so unfair that it helped start the Civil War.

Fast forward 169 years. Last week, two people with a special connection to that case met in Washington, D.C. Lynne Jackson is Dred Scott’s great-great-granddaughter. Charlie Taney is the great-great-grandnephew of Chief Justice Roger Taney, who wrote that terrible ruling. They came together to talk about how race and citizenship are still being debated today.

Just days before their meeting, the Supreme Court made a big decision: almost all babies born in the U.S. are citizens. That’s called birthright citizenship. It comes from the 14th Amendment, which was added after the Civil War to overturn the Dred Scott ruling. But three justices disagreed. Justice Clarence Thomas wrote that the 14th Amendment was only meant for freed slaves and their kids, not everyone.

Lynne Jackson runs a foundation to honor Dred Scott. She says his case was “a major catalyst for the Civil War.” Charlie Taney admitted his ancestor wrote “the single worst decision in the history of the court.” Their meeting reminds us that history isn’t just in the past — it’s still shaping our laws and lives today.
why_it_matters: Decisions made long ago can still touch your life — like who is considered a citizen — and understanding this helps you see why fairness and equality must keep improving.

background_read: Slavery in the United States lasted for more than 200 years before the Civil War (1861-1865). Enslaved African Americans had no rights and could be bought and sold.

Washington, D.C., is the capital city of the United States, where the Supreme Court and many monuments stand. Chief Justice Roger Taney was the head judge who wrote the 1857 ruling that said Black people could not be citizens.
The 14th Amendment was added to the Constitution in 1868 to guarantee citizenship to everyone born in the U.S., directly reversing Taney's decision.
Article_Structure: WHO: Dred Scott (enslaved man), his descendant Lynne Jackson, Charlie Taney (descendant of the judge), and current Supreme Court justices.

WHAT: Two descendants of opposite sides of the famous Dred Scott case met to discuss how race and citizenship are still debated today, shortly after a new Supreme Court ruling on birthright citizenship.
WHERE: Washington, D.C., the capital of the United States.
WHY: The 1857 decision was so unfair that it helped cause the Civil War, and modern disagreements show that its legacy still affects American laws and identity.

perspectives.description: The 14th Amendment fixed the terrible mistake of the Dred Scott case by granting birthright citizenship, showing that the nation can correct its injustices.
Some judges today, like Clarence Thomas, argue that the 14th Amendment was only meant for freed slaves, meaning the debate over citizenship continues.
The meeting between descendants of both sides shows that even painful history can bring people together today to understand and learn, not just to fight.
